specPoints.text: describe the stages in the nitrogen cycle, including the roles of nitrogen fixing bacteria, decomposers, nitrifying bacteria and denitrifying bacteria (specific names of bacteria are not required)

primer.text: Nitrogen gas fills the sky, yet living things cannot absorb it directly. This note walks the nitrogen cycle: fixing bacteria converting gas into nitrates, feeding passing proteins up the food chain, decomposers returning ammonia, and denitrifying bacteria handing nitrogen back to the air.

lessons.title: Fixing Nitrogen for Life
lessons.opening: The air is nearly four-fifths nitrogen gas, yet plants cannot drink it straight from the sky, so nitrogen fixing bacteria first convert that gas into ammonium compounds and then into the nitrates that roots can absorb.
keyPoints: Nitrogen exists as N2 gas in the atmosphere and inside proteins in living tissues.
Nitrogen fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds, which become nitrates in the soil.
Some fixers live free in the soil, while others occupy root nodules of leguminous plants in a mutualistic partnership.
Lightning and fertiliser production can also fix nitrogen, and plants then absorb the nitrates to build proteins.

low.restatement: Bacteria unlock the gas in the air and turn it into soil food for plants.
low.analogy: A currency exchange at the border: cash nobody local accepts is converted into coins every shop will take.
low.examPointer: Name the sequence — nitrogen gas, ammonium compounds, nitrates — and mention the root nodules of leguminous plants.

medium.restatement: Fixation is the gateway of the whole cycle because atmospheric nitrogen is inert: free-living and nodule-dwelling bacteria reduce N2 into ammonium compounds, soil chemistry converts those into nitrates, and roots absorb the nitrates to assemble plant proteins.
medium.analogy: A smithy forging raw ore into nails a carpenter can actually use.
medium.examPointer: For the fixation question, always name the bacterial converters and the final absorbable ion — nitrates.

check.stem: Which molecule holds most of the nitrogen in the atmosphere?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Nitrates live in soil water, not in the air.
Ammonium compounds form after fixation, not in the open sky.
Proteins sit inside living tissues, not in the atmosphere.

check.stem: What do nitrogen fixing bacteria change nitrogen gas into first?

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Nitrites appear later in nitrification, not in fixation.
Plants must build their own proteins from absorbed nitrates.
No rock is made during fixation.

check.stem: How do the bacteria inside root nodules relate to their leguminous host?

options.text: In a mutualistic relationship, fixing nitrogen for both partners
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The partnership feeds both sides; it is not parasitic.
The bacteria actively fix nitrogen for the plant.
Nodule bacteria fix nitrogen; they are not there to decompose.

check.stem: After fixation, which ion do plant roots absorb to build proteins?

options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Plants take up nitrates; ammonium must be converted first.
Leaves cannot drink nitrogen gas; roots take nitrates.
Nitrites are an intermediate step, not the final uptake.

check.stem: Two events beyond bacteria can fix nitrogen. Which pair fits?

options.text: Lightning strikes and the industrial production of fertilisers
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Rain does not split nitrogen gas.
These move water, not nitrogen.
They wear down rock but do not fix nitrogen gas.

check.stem: State the role of nitrogen fixing bacteria.
check.modelAnswer: Nitrogen fixing bacteria convert nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds, which are then changed into nitrates in the soil.

check.stem: Name the structures on leguminous plants that house nitrogen fixing bacteria.
check.modelAnswer: Root nodules on leguminous plants such as peas, beans and clover house the nitrogen fixing bacteria.

check.stem: Explain why plants cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly.
check.modelAnswer: Plants cannot use atmospheric nitrogen directly because nitrogen gas is inert, so it must first be fixed into ammonium compounds and then nitrates that roots can absorb.

check.stem: A farmer sows clover among grass to improve the soil. Explain the benefit.
check.modelAnswer: Clover is leguminous, so the nitrogen fixing bacteria in its root nodules add nitrates to the soil, enriching it for the grass.

lessons.title: Nitrogen Riding the Food Chain
sourceHeadings: Transfer of nitrogen between living organisms
lessons.opening: Once a plant has built protein from nitrates, every bite passes that nitrogen up the food chain, from herbivore to carnivore, one digestive step at a time.
keyPoints: Animals feed on plants and digest the plant proteins, gaining nitrogen for their own animal proteins.
Nitrogen passes from one consumer to the next along the chain in the same fashion.
Every level of the chain depends on the fixed nitrogen that entered through the plants.

low.restatement: Eating passes nitrogen from plants into animals, and from animals into bigger animals.
low.analogy: A parcel handed along a line of couriers, each one adding their own wrapping.
low.examPointer: Say digestion: nitrogen arrives inside proteins and is rebuilt into the proteins of the eater.

medium.restatement: Digestion breaks plant protein into usable nitrogen, which the herbivore rebuilds into animal protein; each predator then repeats the step, so the nitrogen climbs the chain one digestion at a time, anchored by the nitrates plants absorbed.
medium.analogy: A relay where the baton is remade slightly at every handover but never leaves the track.
medium.examPointer: Link the feeding step to protein building — that pairing carries the marks.

check.stem: How does a cow gain nitrogen for building its own proteins?

options.text: By feeding on plants and digesting their proteins
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.

options.text: By absorbing nitrates through its skin
options.explanation: Cow skin cannot soak up soil ions; digestion does the work.
Animals cannot use nitrogen gas by breathing it.
Stream water does not supply usable nitrogen this way.

check.stem: A fox eats a rabbit. What happens to the nitrogen in the rabbit tissues?

options.text: It transfers into the fox, which uses it to build animal proteins
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: It leaves the fox immediately as gas
options.explanation: Nitrogen is built into tissue first, not vented as gas.

options.text: It turns into nitrates inside the fox
options.explanation: Nitrification happens in soil, not inside animal bodies.

options.text: It stays locked in the rabbit forever
options.explanation: Feeding transfers the nitrogen; it does not stay put.

check.stem: Which statement links plant proteins to animal proteins?

options.text: Digested plant proteins supply nitrogen for building animal proteins
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Animal proteins appear spontaneously without nitrogen
options.explanation: All proteins need nitrogen; none appears from nothing.

options.text: Plants convert animal proteins into nitrates
options.explanation: The flow runs from plant tissue into animals, not backwards.

options.text: Nitrogen skips digestion and jumps into muscle
options.explanation: Digestion is the step that unlocks the nitrogen.

check.stem: Why can a top carnivore be described as a store of nitrogen?

options.text: Because nitrogen passed up every feeding step before reaching its body
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: Because it makes nitrogen from sunlight
options.explanation: No animal makes nitrogen from light.

options.text: Because its body traps air in fur
options.explanation: Fur does not store usable nitrogen.

options.text: Because it drinks more water than prey
options.explanation: Water intake is irrelevant to nitrogen storage.

check.stem: In the chain grass, deer, lion, at which step does nitrogen first enter animal tissue?

options.text: At the deer, when it digests grass proteins
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Grass builds plant protein; animal tissue starts with the deer.

options.text: At the lion, straight from the air
options.explanation: The lion gains nitrogen by eating, not from air.

options.text: At no point, animals store no nitrogen
options.explanation: Animal tissue is rich in protein, so it stores nitrogen.

check.stem: State how nitrogen reaches a carnivore in a food chain.
check.modelAnswer: A carnivore gains nitrogen by feeding on other animals, digesting their proteins and using the nitrogen to build its own animal proteins.

check.stem: Name the molecules that animals build using nitrogen from digested food.
check.modelAnswer: Animals build animal proteins from the nitrogen obtained when they digest plant or prey tissue.

check.stem: Explain why every organism in a food chain depends on nitrogen fixation somewhere upstream.
check.modelAnswer: Every organism depends on nitrogen fixation because the chain starts with plants absorbing fixed nitrates, so without that first step no proteins could be built anywhere up the chain.

check.stem: A herbicide wipes out most plants in a meadow. Predict the effect on nitrogen flow to the fox population.
check.modelAnswer: With fewer plants, the herbivores lose their protein source and decline, so the foxes receive less nitrogen through their prey.

lessons.title: Recycling Nitrogen Back to the Air
lessons.opening: Death and waste are not the end of nitrogen: decomposers return it to the soil as ammonia, nitrifying bacteria rebuild it into nitrates, and denitrifying bacteria in waterlogged ground finally hand it back to the air.
keyPoints: Decomposers return nitrogen from dead organisms and waste to the soil as ammonia.
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrites and onwards into nitrates, a process called nitrification.
Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, and they work hardest in anaerobic, waterlogged soil.
Farmers plough soil to add air, which reduces denitrification.

low.restatement: Rotting returns nitrogen to the soil, rebuilding makes it useful again, and denitrifying bacteria send the rest skyward.
low.analogy: A recycling depot: waste dropped off, sorted back into usable stock, and the leftovers shipped out of town.
low.examPointer: Quote the nitrification sequence — ammonia, nitrites, nitrates — and link denitrification to waterlogged soil.

medium.restatement: Decomposers strip nitrogen from corpses and waste into ammonia; nitrifying bacteria oxidise it through nitrites into nitrates for plant uptake; in oxygen-poor ground denitrifying bacteria reduce the nitrates back to nitrogen gas, which ploughing counteracts by aerating the soil.
medium.analogy: A three-stage water filter that can also dump everything back into the river when the drains clog.
medium.examPointer: Name all four bacterial roles — fixing, decomposing, nitrifying, denitrifying — since the spec groups them together.

check.stem: Which organisms return nitrogen from dead tissue to the soil as ammonia?

options.text: Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia onward; the first release is by decomposers.
Denitrifiers send nitrogen back to the air; decomposers put it in the soil.
Nodule bacteria fix nitrogen, they do not release it from dead matter.

check.stem: Put the steps of nitrification in the correct order.

options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
That reverses the real sequence.

options.text: Ammonia, then nitrates, with no intermediate
options.explanation: Nitrites form between ammonia and nitrates.
Ammonia comes first, not after nitrites.

check.stem: In which soil conditions are denitrifying bacteria most active?

options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Airy soil is exactly where denitrifiers slow down.
Cold alone does not define denitrifier habitat; low oxygen does.

options.text: Soil rich in fresh fertiliser only
options.explanation: Nitrates are their substrate, but activity peaks without oxygen.

check.stem: Why do farmers plough their fields?

options.text: Ploughing increases aeration, which reduces denitrification and preserves nitrates
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: To add nitrogen gas to the soil
options.explanation: Ploughing adds air, not nitrogen gas itself.
Farmers want fewer denitrifiers, since they destroy nitrates.
Compaction favours denitrification; ploughing does the opposite.

check.stem: A marshy field loses its nitrate levels over a wet season. Which bacteria caused the loss?

options.text: Denitrifying bacteria converting nitrates back into nitrogen gas
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Fixers add nitrogen compounds; they do not strip nitrates.
Nitrifiers build nitrates, they do not destroy them.
Decomposers release ammonia; the nitrate loss points to denitrifiers.

check.stem: State what nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into.
check.modelAnswer: Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia into nitrites and onwards into nitrates, which plants can absorb.

check.stem: Name the process in which denitrifying bacteria return nitrogen to the atmosphere.
check.modelAnswer: Denitrification is the process in which denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas.

check.stem: Explain why waterlogged soil loses fertility faster than well-drained soil.
check.modelAnswer: Waterlogged soil holds little oxygen, so denitrifying bacteria thrive there and convert nitrates back into nitrogen gas, draining the soil of the nitrates plants need.

check.stem: After a flood, a field stays waterlogged for weeks. Suggest one action and explain it.
check.modelAnswer: Ploughing the field adds air to the soil, which suppresses the anaerobic denitrifying bacteria and protects the remaining nitrates.

glossary.definition: The conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonium compounds by nitrogen fixing bacteria.
The swellings on the roots of leguminous plants that house nitrogen fixing bacteria.
The ions in soil that plant roots absorb to build plant proteins.
The conversion of ammonia into nitrites and onwards into nitrates by nitrifying bacteria.
The conversion of nitrates back into nitrogen gas by denitrifying bacteria.

figures.alt: Diagram illustrating the nitrogen cycle, showing processes like nitrogen fixation, nitrification, denitrification, and the role of plants, animals, and bacteria.
